fable-5.1.text:
Yeah. So I think the honest answer is that the diversity is both smaller and larger than it looks, depending on where you look.

If you look at the pretraining stage, I would actually say there is very little diversity. Everyone is training on more or less the same internet, with more or less the same architecture, with the same objective, which is predict the next token. And when you do that, you're not really expressing yourself as a lab. You're just approximating the distribution of text that humanity has produced. So all the base models are converging toward the same statistical object. They have the same knowledge, they have the same blind spots, they make the same kinds of mistakes. If you squint, they're all one model.

Where the diversity comes from is after that. It's the RL, it's the post-training. And the reason is simple. The pretraining data is given to you by the world. The RL data is something you make. You decide what environments to build, what to reward, what counts as a good answer, what you find annoying. And those decisions reflect the taste of the people in the lab. So in a way each model is a kind of portrait of the people who trained it. One lab likes answers that are very careful, another likes answers that are very direct, another spends its effort on code, and the model picks that up. And these differences get amplified, because RL is a process where small differences in what you reward compound over many steps.

There's an analogy to people, I think. Genetically, humans are nearly identical. The blueprint is the same. And yet two people can be extremely different, because of what they were exposed to and what got reinforced. It's the same thing. Same base, different reinforcement.

And then one more thing I'd add. For a while there was one recipe, which was scale, and when there's one recipe everyone does the same thing, so you get low diversity. I think we're moving into a period where it's less clear what the recipe is. And when it's not clear, different people make different bets. So I'd expect the models to become more different from each other, not less, at least for a while.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining uses “more or less the same internet,” causing base models to converge toward the same statistical object.

r002.rationale: It identifies post-training RL as where diversity comes from, explaining that labs make different choices about what to reward and that those differences shape their models.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the main explanation is actually the lack of diversity, and the reason for that is pre-training. All the pre-trained models are pretty much the same, because they're all trained on more or less the same data: a big slice of the internet, books, code. When everyone uses the same recipe on the same data, you shouldn't be surprised that you get similar things. The models end up with similar knowledge, similar styles, similar strengths, and frankly similar blind spots.

Where differentiation starts to emerge is in RL and post-training. Different companies make different choices about what environments to train on, what to reward, and what they care about. So that's where you see the models start to feel a little different from one another. But even there, people tend to look at the same benchmarks and optimize for similar things, so the pull toward sameness is still quite strong.

If you want genuine diversity, you need some force that actively pushes for it. That's part of why I think ideas like self-play and adversarial setups are interesting. When you have agents competing with each other, or one model trying to find mistakes in another, the incentive to be different is built into the setup. If everyone else is already doing one thing, the way to win is to do something else. That's a very different dynamic from everyone imitating the same data.

It's also why I think, in the longer run, the question of how you get real diversity of thought among AIs is important. With people, you have different upbringings, different experiences, different things they find interesting, and that gives you a team that's better than any single member. With models trained the same way, you don't automatically get that. You'd have to engineer it deliberately, and I don't think we've fully figured out how to do it yet.

r001.rationale: It says pre-trained models are alike because they are trained on more or less the same data, such as internet text, books, and code.

r002.rationale: It identifies differences in RL and post-training choices—such as training environments and rewards—as where model differentiation begins.

fable-5.text:
I think the diversity is actually smaller than you might expect, and it's worth asking why. Pre-training, for everyone, is essentially the same thing: you take the internet, or as much of it as you can get, and you train on it. The data is the same data. So to the degree that models are shaped by pre-training, they are all being pulled toward the same place. That's why there's this feeling that the models are, in some sense, samey — they all have a similar texture, because they're all compressing the same underlying distribution.

Where the diversity comes from is what happens after. The RL training, the post-training — that is not standardized at all. Every company is making its own choices about what environments to build, what rewards to give, what behaviors to encourage. And these choices are much more artisanal. Someone at the company decides, we want the model to behave this way, we're going to build this kind of RL environment, we're going to emphasize this kind of task. There is a person, or a team, with opinions, and those opinions get imprinted on the model. That is where the personality differences come from, where one model feels one way to talk to and another feels different.

So you could say: pre-training is where the models converge, and RL is where they diverge. And I think this also tells you something about the current state of the field. If the field were more mature, if there were a well-understood, principled way to do this part of training, you would expect the diversity to shrink again, because everyone would do the thing that works. The fact that the models differ as much as they do is a sign that we're still in the phase where people are making it up — trying things, following taste. The diversity is a measure of how much is still not understood.

r001.rationale: It says pre-training uses essentially the same internet data, which pulls models toward the same place and gives them a similar texture.

r002.rationale: It identifies nonstandard RL and post-training choices across companies as the source of model differences.

opus-5.text:
It's a good question, and I think the first thing to say is that the diversity is actually smaller than people expect. If you look at the models from the different labs, they are far more similar to each other than they are different. And that's the thing that needs explaining first.

The reason, I think, is that there is essentially one pretraining dataset. There's one internet. Everyone is training on more or less the same text, with somewhat different filtering and somewhat different mixtures, but the underlying distribution is shared. And on top of that, everyone is reading the same papers, hiring from the same pool of people, and the architecture space that actually works at scale is quite narrow. So you have strong convergent pressure. The model is, in some sense, a function of the data, and if the data is the same, you get something similar.

Then, within that, the diversity you do see comes mostly from post-training, and from taste. The choices about what the model should be like, which behaviors you reinforce, which environments you train on, how you handle the cases where the human raters disagree — those are judgment calls, and different teams have different judgment, different aesthetic preferences. That's where the personality lives. If you talk to the models for a while you can tell them apart, and what you're detecting is not really a difference in capability, it's a difference in what the people who trained them wanted.

I'll add one more thing. I expect the diversity to increase, not decrease, as the field moves away from pretraining as the dominant source of capability. Pretraining is the great homogenizer, because the data is fixed and there's only so much of it. Once the bulk of the learning comes from the model interacting with things — environments, tasks, whatever it ends up being — those setups are designed, and design choices diverge. Different labs will make very different bets, and the models will reflect that much more strongly than they do now.

r001.rationale: The response says the labs use essentially the same pretraining dataset and shared underlying text distribution, which explains why their models are similar.

r002.rationale: It attributes differences to post-training choices, including which behaviors teams reinforce and how they handle disagreements among human raters, identifying differing reinforcement and feedback practices as a source of differentiation.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think part of the answer is pre-training. It's the same recipe and roughly the same data for everyone: the internet, books, code, whatever you can get. If you train big neural nets on essentially the same data with the same objective, you'll get models that end up similar in a lot of ways. So the surprising thing to me is how much similarity there is, and I'd say that's more the default than the diversity.

Where the differences come from is mostly after that, in post-training and RL. Each company builds its own environments and decides what to reward and what to optimize for. That's where the models start to develop different characters, and it's also where a lot of human judgment and taste goes in.

Within a single company, though, I think the diversity is much lower than people would like. If you sample from the same model many times, you often get variations on the same thing, and that's different from having a group of people who think in different ways. People are diverse partly because they've had different experiences and different training, and partly because they've learned to specialize and be different from each other.

That's one reason I find ideas like self-play interesting. When agents compete with each other, each one is incentivized to find a different approach, because doing the same thing as the other agent isn't very useful. So you get a way to turn compute into diversity of strategy without needing new data. I'm not saying that's the whole answer. But I think any serious explanation has to start from the fact that the data is mostly shared, and the real divergence only begins when you change what the model is being optimized for.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training uses roughly the same data across models and links that shared data to their similarity.

r002.rationale: It identifies post-training and RL as where models diverge, citing differing environments, rewards, and optimization choices.

haiku-5.5.text:
Part of it is that the models are trained on a lot of the same material, so you'd expect convergence. But the differences come from choices made at every stage. Each lab curates its own data mixture, and those decisions about what to include, filter out, or upweight matter a lot. Then there's post-training, where the target behavior gets shaped through human feedback, constitutions, or reinforcement learning. That's where personality and style really diverge.

I'd also say we still understand the mapping from those choices to the final model's character only loosely. Two models can share a broad recipe and end up with very different tendencies, and small changes in the reward signal can ripple out in ways nobody predicted. So the diversity is partly intentional and partly the result of a process we don't fully control.

What interests me more is whether that diversity converges over time or stays. If the underlying capabilities keep converging, the remaining differences will be in values, judgment, and how the model reasons about uncertainty. That's the part I think we should be paying the most attention to.

r001.rationale: The response says the models are trained on “a lot of the same material,” which it connects to expected convergence.

r002.rationale: It identifies post-training choices, including reinforcement learning, as shaping model behavior, and says changes in the reward signal can produce different tendencies.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there are two forces pulling in opposite directions. If you train models on similar data, with similar objectives, you should expect them to learn many of the same things. They’re trying to explain the same world. So there’s a strong force toward similarity.

But the training objective doesn’t uniquely specify the model. There are many ways to do well at predicting the next word, and the choices you make during training can favor different solutions. Then post-training can make those differences much more visible—what the model is willing to say, how it approaches a problem, how it expresses uncertainty.

So I would distinguish diversity in behavior from diversity in underlying capability. Two models can feel quite different when you talk to them and still have very similar strengths and weaknesses.

r001.rationale: The response says models trained on similar data should learn many of the same things, explaining their similarity.

r002.rationale: It says training choices and post-training can make models differ, but does not identify differences in reinforcement-learning training as a source.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think you have to distinguish two kinds of diversity. There’s diversity in personality—how the model talks, whether it’s more cautious, more direct. And then there’s diversity in how it actually thinks about a problem. Those are not necessarily the same thing.

You could imagine two models that sound quite different but solve the same problems and make the same mistakes. Or two models that sound similar but have quite different strengths.

My guess is that a lot depends on how similar their training is. If you use similar data and similar training methods, there’s a strong force pushing you toward similar results. But the training doesn’t uniquely determine everything. There are different solutions that work on the data, and those differences can become visible when you ask something new.

So the interesting question is: when one model fails, how likely is another model to succeed? That tells you something deeper about diversity than whether they have different conversational styles.

r001.rationale: The response says similar data and training methods tend to produce similar results, but does not attribute similarity to models being trained on essentially the same data.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify differences in reinforcement-learning training as a source of post-training differentiation.

sol-6.text: I think the surprising thing is that these models learn from a very broad and imperfectly specified signal. There are many ways to fit that signal, and the choices made during training—what data the model sees, what it is rewarded for, and how it is tuned afterward—can push it toward quite different behaviors. So even if two models look similar in broad outline, I would expect them to develop different strengths, habits, and ways of answering.

r001.rationale: The response says models can look similar in broad outline, but does not attribute that similarity to being trained on essentially the same data.

r002.rationale: The response mentions rewards and later tuning as possible sources of different behavior, but does not identify differences in reinforcement-learning training during post-training.

terra-5.6.text: I think it’s because the training process is surprisingly chaotic. Tiny differences in initialization, data order, and optimization get amplified, and there are many different ways to represent the same underlying regularities in the data. So even models trained very similarly can end up with noticeably different personalities, strengths, and blind spots.

r001.rationale: The response attributes model differences to training variability and shared ways of representing data regularities; it does not say pre-trained models are similar because they use essentially the same data.

r002.rationale: The response mentions optimization generally but does not identify differences in reinforcement-learning training as a source of post-training differentiation.

sol-5.6.text: I think a lot of the apparent diversity comes from post-training. The base models may be more similar than they seem, but different choices about which behaviors to reward, which answers to discourage, and how the model should interact with users can produce quite different personalities and capabilities. There are also differences in data and architecture, but post-training makes those differences especially visible.

r001.rationale: The response says base models may be more similar, but does not attribute that similarity to being trained on essentially the same data.

r002.rationale: The response points to different post-training choices about rewarded or discouraged behaviors, but does not identify reinforcement-learning training as the source of differentiation.

luna-5.6.text:
There’s more diversity than you might expect, even though many of these models are trained on overlapping data. The data mixture, filtering, architecture, optimization details, and random initialization all matter. Small differences early in training can get amplified, so the models end up developing different internal representations and different ways of generalizing.

Then post-training introduces another major source of diversity. The choice of demonstrations, human preferences, reward models, safety policies, and product objectives can push models toward different personalities and behaviors. So the underlying capabilities may overlap substantially, but the models can still differ in what they notice, how they reason, what they refuse to do, and how they express an answer. I suspect that as we understand training better, we’ll be able to deliberately create much more diversity rather than getting it mostly as a byproduct.

r001.rationale: The response mentions overlapping training data, but says data-mixture differences matter and does not attribute pre-trained models’ similarity to essentially the same data.

r002.rationale: The response identifies post-training choices such as demonstrations, preferences, and reward models as sources of diversity, but does not identify differences in reinforcement-learning training.

luna-6.text: I think it comes from the fact that there are many different ways to build a very capable language model. You can change the data, the architecture, the training process, and especially the way you shape the model after pretraining. Even small differences can lead to different personalities and strengths, because the objective leaves a lot of room for the model to learn different things.

r001.rationale: The response says models can differ in their data, but does not attribute similarities among pretrained models to being trained on essentially the same data.

r002.rationale: It mentions differing training processes and post-pretraining shaping, but does not identify reinforcement-learning training as a source of differentiation.
